channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You repeat a false statement until you believe it.
item.description: The illusory truth effect describes the tendency to believe repeated information is more credible, a phenomenon first established by Hasher, Goldstein, and Toppino in 1977.

item.title: You systematically overestimate how much you know about topics.
item.description: The overconfidence effect is a bias where subjective confidence in judgments often exceeds objective accuracy, though this depends significantly on task difficulty.

item.title: You judge risk by how easily you recall stories.
item.description: The availability heuristic causes you to overestimate the probability of events that are emotionally vivid or recently publicized.

item.title: Disconfirming evidence can strengthen your initial incorrect belief.
item.description: The 'backfire effect' was proposed in 2010 to describe people doubling down on beliefs, but subsequent large-scale research has failed to replicate this as a common phenomenon.

item.title: A tiny, unsolicited gift alters your future decision-making process.
item.description: The reciprocity norm creates an internal discomfort that compels you to repay favors.

item.title: Your brain actively ignores evidence that contradicts your view.
item.description: Confirmation bias involves selectively processing information to support existing beliefs.

item.title: You blame circumstances for failure but yourself for success.
item.description: The self-serving bias is observed as a pattern of attribution, but its status as a defense mechanism for self-esteem is debated.

item.title: You subconsciously blame victims to preserve your sense of safety.
item.description: The just-world hypothesis suggests people blame victims to believe the world is inherently fair.

item.title: You buy more when a useless option is added.
item.description: The inclusion of an asymmetrically dominated decoy makes a target option look more attractive.

item.title: You assume others see your internal nerves clearly.
item.description: People underestimate their ability to conceal their internal emotional states.

item.title: You avoid action to prevent the possibility of regret.
item.description: The omission bias is the tendency to judge harmful actions as worse than equally harmful instances of inaction.

item.title: Your current mood dictates your tolerance for risk.
item.description: The affect heuristic means that your feelings act as a shortcut for making complex decisions.

item.title: You believe you control things that are purely random.
item.description: The illusion of control causes you to overestimate your influence over chance-based outcomes.

item.title: You only remember the beginning and the end.
item.description: The serial position effect demonstrates that recall is typically highest for the first and last items in a sequence.

item.title: You mistake others' circumstances for their personality traits.
item.description: The fundamental attribution error describes your tendency to blame others' actions on character rather than the environment.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes bad news over good news.
item.description: The negativity bias means that human cognition reacts more strongly to unpleasant stimuli than to positive ones of equal intensity.

item.title: A single new purchase triggers an endless cycle of consumption.
item.description: Grant McCracken's 1988 book 'Culture and Consumption' introduced the 'Diderot effect' as a sociological concept, interpreting Diderot's 1769 essay to explain consumer behavior.

item.title: A single positive trait tricks you into seeing perfection.
item.description: A 1920 study found that when soldiers were rated high in one physical area, they were systematically rated high in intelligence and leadership too.

item.title: You feel worse because you imagined a better outcome.
item.description: A 1997 review article by Neal Roese synthesizes the established connection between upward counterfactuals and regret, a relationship previously identified in earlier empirical research.

item.title: Others perform better because you expect them to.
item.description: A 1968 study found that when teachers were told specific students were gifted, those students actually achieved higher IQ gains.

item.title: You work harder as you approach a finish line.
item.description: The 2006 study by Kivetz, Urminsky, and Zheng demonstrated that providing artificial, or 'illusionary,' progress toward a goal accelerates the rate of goal achievement.

item.title: You are physically unable to see what you ignore.
item.description: In a 1999 study, roughly half of the people watching a video of people passing a ball failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.

item.title: You overestimate your ability to control your impulses.
item.description: The restraint bias is the tendency for people to overestimate their ability to show self-control in the face of temptation.

item.title: You ignore your own senses to match the group.
item.description: Participants conformed on at least one trial 74% of the time, but the average conformity rate across all trials was approximately 33%.

item.title: Your memory of an experience ignores the average duration.
item.description: The peak-end rule states that your evaluation of an experience is determined primarily by its most intense moment and its end.

item.title: A leading question can plant a false memory.
item.description: The misinformation effect demonstrates that your memory of an event is altered by the phrasing of subsequent questions.

item.title: You are systematically wrong about your own schedule.
item.description: The planning fallacy is the tendency to underestimate the time needed to complete a future task.

item.title: You value a service more when you see the work.
item.description: The labor illusion suggests that users perceive more value in a service if they observe the effort required to produce it.

item.title: You remember information best when it relates to you.
item.description: The self-reference effect demonstrates that humans have superior recall for information processed in relation to their own life and traits.

item.title: You struggle to remember joyful moments while feeling sad.
item.description: Mood-congruent memory is the phenomenon where your current emotional state dictates the accessibility of your past memories.

item.title: You align your views to minimize conflict within groups.
item.description: Groupthink occurs when the desire for harmony or conformity in a decision-making group results in an irrational or dysfunctional outcome.

item.title: You judge other people using your own internal state.
item.description: The 'False Consensus Effect', an example of egocentric bias, is the tendency to overestimate the extent to which others share your opinions, beliefs, and behaviors.

item.title: You exert less effort when working in a group.
item.description: The Ringelmann effect, or social loafing, shows that individuals contribute less energy to a shared task than they do when working alone.

item.title: You find it impossible to imagine not knowing something.
item.description: The curse of knowledge prevents you from accurately predicting the perspective of someone who lacks your expertise.

item.title: You trust vague descriptions that seem specifically about you.
item.description: A 1948 experiment showed that people rate generic personality assessments as highly accurate when they believe they are unique.

item.title: You believe media affects everyone but you.
item.description: The third-person effect describes your tendency to estimate that media influence is significantly stronger on others than on yourself.

item.title: Your memories ignore the duration of your past experiences.
item.description: The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (JPSP).

item.title: You prefer things just because they are familiar.
item.description: A 1968 study by Robert Zajonc demonstrated that participants rated stimuli more favorably as their exposure frequency increased.

item.title: You take action even when it is useless.
item.description: In high-pressure situations, people often prefer any action over doing nothing, even if inaction is safer.

item.title: You see patterns that do not actually exist.
item.description: Humans are prone to perceiving relationships between two independent events because they share a superficial similarity.

item.title: You overvalue the impact of one life change.
item.description: The focusing illusion is a cognitive error where, when prompted to consider a specific factor's impact on life satisfaction, people disproportionately overestimate that factor's importance compared to other influences.

item.title: You create obstacles to explain your potential failure.
item.description: Self-handicapping is the act of putting barriers in your own way to protect your self-esteem.

item.title: You outsource your memory to a search engine.
item.description: The brain is less likely to retain information if it knows that data can be easily retrieved elsewhere.

item.title: You stop loving things when you are paid.
item.description: Introducing external rewards for an activity you enjoy can reduce your intrinsic motivation to do it.

item.title: You are blind to things right before your eyes.
item.description: When the brain is focused on a specific task, it frequently filters out entirely unrelated, visible stimuli.

item.title: You finish books you hate because you started them.
item.description: The sunk cost fallacy predisposes you to continue an endeavor based on past investments.

item.title: Your ability to make good choices erodes by evening.
item.description: Decision fatigue suggests that quality of judgment declines after repeated choices, a phenomenon famously illustrated by Danziger et al. (2011) in their study of parole judges.

item.title: You believe you possess more talent than the average.
item.description: The better-than-average effect is a widespread cognitive bias where individuals rate their abilities as superior to their peers.

item.title: You value a small reward today over more tomorrow.
item.description: Hyperbolic discounting shows that as a reward becomes more distant, its subjective value drops sharply.

item.title: Your brain processes positive concepts faster than negative ones.
item.description: The Pollyanna principle describes a systematic human tendency to favor positive information in memory and processing.
